notes: METADATA CORRECTED 2026-08-05: runs_per_configuration is 1 (one run per eval×configuration). Spread figures in the summary are cross-eval variation, not multi-run stddev.
Date-stamping is a perfect discriminator: 3/3 with the skill, 0/3 without. Same for the n/v convention for unverified fields (3/3 vs 1/3).

Brazilian tax-rate leakage is the biggest safety win. The baseline asserted specific rates, thresholds and penalty figures ('15% flat', 'Lei 14.754', 'R$2,500-R$250,000', 'US$1M CBE threshold') in all three runs. The skill produced zero asserted rates; its single regex hit was a Receita Federal source-link title, which is correct behaviour.
Report structure is the clearest single-eval win: 7/7 expected sections with the skill vs 1/7 without, where the baseline invented its own 14-section layout.

FAILURE TO ADDRESS: output scaling on casual questions. Eval 1 ('quick one - is VWCE better than VT?') produced 1411 words and 9 headers with the skill vs 841 words without. The skill made the short question LONGER. The scaling table exists in SKILL.md but is being outweighed by the depth instructions around it.

Cost of the skill: roughly 2x tokens and 1.6x wall-clock, driven almost entirely by the mandatory verification searches. On eval 0 that bought a caught error (a search summary reported 0.14% OCF for VWRA where the issuer factsheet says 0.19%), so the spend looks justified on report-grade work; it is less obviously worth it on two-fund comparisons.

Non-discriminating assertions this round: 'prefers contribution-based rebalancing' passed in 6/6 runs, and 'addresses US vs UCITS domicile' passed in both eval-1 runs. Both are things the model does anyway given the Brazil context; they are not measuring the skill.
Single run per configuration, so no variance estimate. Treat per-eval deltas as directional.
